epistemology.label: Historical epistemology
epistemology.description: Here the label denotes the French tradition associated with Bachelard and Canguilhem: histories of scientific concepts, norms, and discontinuities. It informs Foucault through a route distinct from structural linguistics. It is not an umbrella for every historical or sociological account of scientific knowledge. Bachelard’s own preliminary discourse distinguishes normative epistemology from a chronological history and calls its period labels approximate. Canguilhem’s norm/average discussion draws on Halbwachs and human geography; his later preface distinguishes newly encountered works from resources actually used in1943.
epistemology.representative_figures_and_works: French history and philosophy of science; this connection prevents treating Foucault as merely a descendant of structural linguistics. Bachelard, La formation de l’esprit scientifique (1938); Canguilhem, the normal/pathological essay (1943; expanded 1966) and La formation du concept de réflexe (1955).

political.label: Political history
political.description: Examines institutions, diplomacy and struggles over power through different methods. Namier reconstructs parliamentary connections; Benson studies voters; Tilly investigates collective claims; Hunt joins political symbols and social identities. Hill, Dorothy Thompson and Flexner examine radical and rights politics, while Guha and Cooper investigate insurgency and labor under colonial rule. These approaches overlap without replacing all earlier political history.

Further contexts: Namier (1929), Flexner (1959), William Appleman Williams (1959), Hill (1972), Guha (1983), Tilly (1986) and Cooper (1996).

political.scope_note: Diplomatic, institutional, social, and cultural political histories persist and interact; the field did not disappear with the rise of social history. Distinguish institutional elites, electoral categories, popular organization and colonial subjects. Cultural political history can retain social and quantitative evidence; attention to popular action does not make all movements democratic. Regional examples are selective, not a globally complete political canon.

strands.title: The new political history of Britain, 1993–2011
strands.focus: After the Social History round on Stedman Jones (1992–93), British political history took the linguistic turn and argued with it. Vernon's Politics and the People (1993) held that between the Reform Acts 'the official political subject was redefined in the image of print' and the public sphere narrowed (p. 107, as quoted by Tilly); his Re-reading the Constitution (1996) gathered Epstein, Wahrman, Joyce, Antony Taylor and Anna Clark under 'new narratives'. Vernon credited Epstein's late-1980s articles, subsequently collected in Radical Expression (1994), as inspirational 'for those like myself who followed into the field' of 'the new cultural history of British politics' (2004). Lawrence and Taylor's Party, State and Society (1997) set out to 'examine critically "electoral sociology"' (as quoted by LoPatin), and Lawrence's Speaking for the People (1998) questioned 'the rise of class politics' and 'the triumph of party' for the politics of place and gender; Vernon found it 'ambitious, but ultimately flawed' (1999) and Lawrence answered, in a response posted in 2010, that 'realist' and 'constructivist' approaches must be combined. Electing Our Masters (2009) followed the hustings and the platform; in 2011 Lawrence argued for a 'conservative' rather than 'liberal' modernity. Positions within one field, not a school; the debate entry languages_of_class holds the exchanges.
strands.works: Vernon, Politics and the People (1993), ed., Re-reading the Constitution (1996); Epstein, Radical Expression (1994); Lawrence and Taylor, eds, Party, State and Society (1997); Lawrence, Speaking for the People (1998), Electing Our Masters (2009), 'Paternalism, Class, and the British Path to Modernity' (2011); Vernon's review and Lawrence's response (Reviews in History, 1999/2010)

biography.scope_note: A genre and set of methods with ancient and varied roots, not inherently great-man history, psychohistory or microstoria. The selected roster combines earlier practices, modern historical work and critics. Davis’s comparison preserves religious and colonial differences; her imagined prologue is not historical testimony. Bourdieu questions narrated coherence without banning life histories; Levi emphasizes choices within constraints and investigates group formation. Biography can explain wider relations, but its scale and source gaps remain subjects of criticism. Non-European traditions and original translation witnesses require further research; the current selection is not exhaustive.

post.label: Postcolonial history / critique

memory.scope_note: Halbwachs’s social frameworks, Nora’s commemorative sites, and Samuel’s popular uses of the past are distinct projects. Communicative and cultural memory are the Assmann project’s distinctions, not a universal taxonomy. War mourning, Holocaust memorials and feminist subjectivity require different historical explanations; this selection remains weighted toward European debates. Jelin’s Argentina project adds a pre-2000 case beyond Europe; it does not represent all Latin American memory work.

strands.title: Social frameworks of remembering

strands.works: Les cadres sociaux de la mémoire (1925); English selections (1992)

strands.title: Sites of memory and historical reconstruction
strands.focus: Sites combine material, symbolic and functional dimensions, extending beyond monuments alone.

strands.title: Habit, bodies and ceremony
strands.focus: Remembering includes bodily competence, not only recalled propositions or pictures.

strands.title: Communication and cultural objectivation
strands.focus: Everyday recollection and durable cultural forms operate differently; Assmann revises rather than merely repeats Halbwachs.

strands.title: Media and uses of cultural memory
strands.focus: Writing, images and monuments organize what can be stored and recalled.

strands.title: Mourning and cultural continuities after war
strands.focus: Traditional and modern forms overlap in Great War mourning; this is not a template for every subsequent catastrophe.
strands.works: Sites of Memory, Sites of Mourning (1995)

strands.title: Holocaust memorials and their contexts
strands.focus: Memorial forms and meanings vary across places and institutions.

strands.title: Popular practices of historical knowledge
strands.focus: Family research, images and reenactment make historical work visible outside professional writing.

strands.title: Life histories, gender and subjectivity
strands.focus: Fascist everyday life and feminist psychoanalytic inquiry are distinct routes into interpreted recollection.

strands.title: Archival authority, access and inscription
strands.focus: Combe’s inquiry into access supplies a named resource to Derrida. His account differentiates archives from spontaneous memory and examines institutional authority and technical inscription. From the archival profession, Schwartz and Cook called archives 'active sites where social power is negotiated' whose appraisal and access shape collective memory (2002, abstract); the wider readership is on the entry archival_turn.

strands.title: Urban landscapes and public memory
strands.focus: Hayden’s collaborative practice links historical interpretation to lived places.

strands.title: Traditions in contact and conflict
strands.focus: Halbwachs explains revisions of collective remembering through contact with other groups and their traditions; social frameworks are not an assurance of a unanimous or unchanging past.
strands.works: Les cadres sociaux de la mémoire (1925), final concluding subsection

strands.title: Memorial production and public disagreement
strands.focus: Young’s Saarbrücken account follows a covert art project into public controversy and political recognition. His interpretation makes the memorial’s production and reception part of its meaning.

strands.title: Vichy’s afterlife and historical inquiry

strands.title: Resources for studying forgetting

indigenous.scope_note: A selective grouping of independently rooted Indigenous historical practices and decolonizing research, with Andean, Haudenosaunee, Ojibwe, Cree, Métis, Wendat, Māori, Osage, Native Hawaiian, Yukon and Australian examples. Earlier writing, community knowledge, academic historical scholarship and decolonizing methodology have different histories. Community historians, academic historians and outside collaborators have different positions. Neither anthropology nor European theory is their common origin; no selection stands for every nation or protocol. Membership is a contextual intellectual contribution, not a binary Indigenous-identity classification. Journal counts are venue-based publication proxies and cannot date the origins of these practices or identify Indigenous authorship. Academic Indigenous history includes documented collaborations with scholars working across historical, anthropological and geographical inquiries. Shared research subjects do not establish intellectual descent. Later source dates are separate from earlier events; only Leddy’s 2010 article is accepted here as a selected post-2000 intervention.

philhistory.description: Disputes concern general laws, understanding actions, historical facts, and the possibility of objectivity. Narrative theory enters a discussion already under way.

strands.title: Genealogy, values and historical explanation
strands.focus: Nietzsche’s critique asks both how moral judgments arise and what they are worth; Rée and Schopenhauer are distinct interlocutors. Origin and later function must not be conflated.

strands.title: Rhetoric, reference and historical achievement
strands.focus: Barthes analyzes the presentation of reality; Bann uses that analysis while questioning its scope and preserving source-based scrutiny. Formal analysis alone does not decide a historical claim’s truth.

strands.title: The historian, surviving sources and the historical picture
strands.focus: Michelet’s account of reciprocal formation and Huizinga’s warning about surviving art raise different questions about historical knowledge; they do not deny the need for evidence.

strands.title: Evidence, understanding and the historical question
strands.focus: Droysen, Dilthey, Croce and Collingwood offer different accounts of what inquiry does with traces, thought, context and practical concerns. These are explicit conceptual resources, not a common doctrine or a proved genealogy of later debate.

strands.title: Language use and following rules
strands.focus: Wittgenstein examines varied activities and similarities rather than one essence of language. Following a rule involves a practice; an interpretation cannot supply its own application without limit.

strands.title: Knowing how, action and accomplishment
strands.focus: Ryle distinguishes competent action from both an automatic movement and a performance governed by an endless series of prior theoretical decisions. A richer action description identifies purpose and circumstances.
strands.works: The Concept of Mind, II.1–3; The Thinking of Thoughts

strands.title: Narrative and historical understanding
strands.focus: White identifies particular philosophical interlocutors rather than responding to one undifferentiated philosophy of history.

strands.title: Laws, probability and explanation sketches
strands.focus: Hempel’s demand for testable relations permits incomplete research proposals and probabilistic accounts.

strands.title: Action and the limits of one explanatory model
strands.focus: Dray’s challenge includes reasons, uniqueness and pragmatic questions; it is not a ban on all generalization.
strands.works: Laws and Explanation (1957); Nature of Historical Explanation (1952)

strands.title: Selection, relevance and revisable interpretation
strands.focus: Becker and Carr preserve evidence while disputing self-interpreting facts; they do not offer identical positions.

strands.title: Historical craft, imagination and instruction
strands.focus: Elton’s research/writing/teaching agenda and Skinner’s apprenticeship reading identify practices of training.

strands.title: Narrative comprehension and truth
strands.focus: Mink separates grasping relations from truth tests and disputes both Gallie’s following and Hardy’s lived-narrative account.

strands.title: Knowledge of the past and speculative historical systems
strands.focus: Walsh’s scope distinguishes questions about inquiry from philosophies of the whole historical process.

Journal milestones mark consolidation, not the first historical study of cities.

Institutions, cultural boundaries and political conflicts help explain how a shared class identity was made. This selected introduction adds an urban elite-formation problem alongside existing histories of neighbourhoods, mobility and racial inequality; it does not replace them.

spatialhistory.date_label: Sauer 1925 · Hoskins 1955 · critical spatial studies and historical GIS by the 1990s
spatialhistory.description: Investigates how places, landscapes, territories and spatial relationships are made and transformed through time. Reconstructing past geographies, interpreting maps and colonial naming, tracing contested place identities, and linking historical records through GIS are different practices within this broad field.

spatialhistory.scope_note: Historical geography has roots well before digital mapping. Spatial history is an overlapping set of approaches, not a synonym for GIS or one unified school. The existing Geography & environmental inquiry entry retains its wider intellectual resources. This selection foregrounds British reconstruction, Australian colonial space and a British HGIS project; wider regional traditions and Indigenous spatial knowledge require fuller treatment. Later digital projects are not backdated into the period reviewed through 2000.

strands.focus: Darby works from Domesday evidence; the extent of a source is not identical to the geography of a whole society.

strands.title: Producing space through social practice and power
strands.focus: Lefebvre’s 1974 introduction asks how spaces and their codes are produced and changed through social practices, planning and power. Space participates in these relations rather than merely containing them. This is his theoretical proposal; the excerpt neither supplies a GIS procedure nor establishes a uniform school of spatial historians.
strands.works: La production de l’espace (1974), introduction excerpt pp. 19–27; The Production of Space, trans. Donald Nicholson-Smith (1991, metadata only)

strands.title: Uneven sovereignty: legal corridors and enclaves
strands.focus: Benton follows the relation between geographic descriptions, mobile subjects and delegated jurisdiction. Imperial space appears as differentiated corridors and enclaves; her account asks how these arrangements changed rather than treating all places as equally controlled or every legal anomaly as a temporary failure. The book’s full cases and later chapters remain unread here.
strands.works: A Search for Sovereignty (2010 imprint), introduction pp. 1–5 and 7–10; Humanity interview (2011), selected Benton answers.
